content: 1. Easy access to differentiated antiretroviral therapy (ART) delivery models, along with at least one viral load test showing <1000 copies/mL in the past three months, and access to antenatal care are essential for effective HIV management in pregnant women. 2. Women who initiate ART during pregnancy become eligible for differentiated ART delivery models only in the postpartum period. Additional requirements include a negative HIV nucleic acid test (NAT) result for their infant at six weeks and evidence of accessing infant follow-up care. 3. Successful treatment of children, particularly younger ones, requires caregivers to understand the critical importance of adherence to treatment and retention in care. Factors influencing adherence include appropriate antiretroviral (ARV) drug formulations, centralized pediatric care, adequate psychosocial support, and effective disclosure of HIV status to children. 4. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends age-appropriate disclosure of HIV status to children. This process can be supported by adherence counseling, appointment reminders, psychosocial support to address stigma and fear, and assisted disclosure strategies. Caregivers should be encouraged to disclose HIV status to children early, using age-appropriate messaging and tools. 5. Adolescents face unique barriers to care, including frequent clinic visits, stigma, long waiting times, and school absences. Negative attitudes from healthcare workers, privacy concerns, and limited opportunities to discuss their concerns further hinder retention. Distance to facilities and out-of-pocket expenses also restrict engagement. 6. Service delivery models that extend beyond healthcare facilities, such as peer-based interventions and community-based services, are highly valued by adolescents and should be considered. Flexible appointment systems accommodating school hours, comprehensive services addressing psychosocial and sexual health needs, and proactive follow-up strategies are recommended. 7. Men receiving ART have a 46% higher risk of death compared to women, partly due to late diagnosis and delayed ART initiation. Men in high HIV burden settings and key populations are less likely to know their HIV status. WHO emphasizes the need to improve HIV testing coverage among men, particularly in high-burden settings and key populations. 8. Community and peer-based service delivery options are critical for supporting retention in care, especially in settings where individuals face criminalization due to their behavior or identity. For people in prisons or closed settings, ensuring continuity of care through measures like providing two months of ART upon community reintegration is essential. 9. Tracing and re-engagement interventions are recommended to support individuals who have disengaged from care. These interventions include remote communication (phone, text, email), in-person tracing, and a combination of approaches. Tracing is more effective when initiated soon after a missed visit. 10. Tracing activities can successfully re-engage individuals in care and achieve viral load suppression. While there is a small risk of inadvertent HIV status disclosure, the benefits of re-engagement outweigh the risks. A non-judgmental approach and respect for confidentiality are essential. 11. Task sharing in ART initiation and maintenance involves redistributing clinical tasks to trained non-physician clinicians, midwives, nurses, and community health workers. Evidence shows comparable clinical outcomes and improved retention when these healthcare workers perform ART-related tasks. 12. Community health workers can dispense and distribute ART between regular clinical visits, ensuring continuity of care. Training, mentoring, and supervision are critical to maintaining the quality of care. 13. Research is needed to evaluate the cost and effectiveness of community-level interventions in different settings. Tailored support addressing the reasons for disengagement is essential to minimize care interruptions and support re-engagement. 14. Programs should routinely disaggregate data by sex to monitor access and treatment outcomes for men and women. Understanding local and general reasons for retention failures is more predictive than sociodemographic factors like age and sex. 15. Interventions to support re-engagement in care should include peer or healthcare provider outreach, reminders, economic incentives, and case management. Confidentiality must be ensured, and clients should consent to tracing during ART initiation discussions. 16. The WHO strongly recommends community support for people living with HIV to improve retention in care. Poor retention undermines program outcomes, including reduced mortality and sustained viral load suppression. 17. The Welcome Back service in South Africa, established by Médecins Sans Frontières and the Department of Health, exemplifies a successful approach combining medical and psychosocial support for individuals who have disengaged from care.
